notes: A writing streak now counts every day you write anything, whether or not you reach your daily goal.
Today's words, your goal and your streak are shared with NorthRay Launcher's home page (a small file on this PC only).

Fixed: clicking OK (or any button) in a question box did nothing when Windows' display scaling was above 100%; only Enter worked. The box was drawn smaller than the places it took clicks. This is what stopped Review › Names › “Change to” from working with the mouse.

Fixed: “Change to” now changes every use of the name, including ones in curly quotes (“Marren, wait!”), with a possessive (Marren’s), or next to a dash or an ellipsis. Before, those were skipped. “Appears in” counts them too.

Choosing who a relationship is with (and a parent, partner, brother or sister, or child) now has a search field: type part of a name and the list narrows. Long lists scroll with the mouse wheel or Page Up and Page Down, so every entry can be reached.
Any long pop-up list in Writing Studio works the same way.

Right-click a name in Writing: “Add “Maren” to the bible…” (as whichever kind), or “Open “Maren” in the bible” when it's there. A name of several words (“Maren Holt”) is taken whole, or select the words you want.
New names as you write: Writing's panel lists names in the open chapter that aren't in the bible yet, with “Add to the bible…” and “Not a name”.

Maps: a place's or realm's page can have a map, any picture you've made. “+ Pin an entry…” and a click on the map puts it there; click a pin to open it, move it or take it off. Places lists your maps.

Checks (Worldbuilding's sidebar): names spelt like a bible name, facts that disagree (two lines of an entry's details, or its eyes, hair or age against what the text says about them), and entries never named in the text. Anything can be marked as fine.
Glossary (Worldbuilding's sidebar): every name and other name from A to Z, with how it's said (“How it's said” on each page) and its line or two.
Magic and powers: a kind of its own, with pages for how it works, its rules, costs and limits, who can use it and what it can't do.
Spoilers: mark any fact (a detail, a section, the summary, or the whole entry) as revealed in a later book. The page shows it, and a reader's guide leaves it out for readers of earlier books.

Share the bible: a website (a folder of linked pages, with the glossary, families, relationships, maps and galleries, ready to put online), or a printable bible as a PDF, typeset like a book. Either can be everything, or a reader's guide up to the end of a chosen book, without spoilers from later books or your notes.

Family trees: a character's page has a Family section with their parents, partners, brothers and sisters, and children (anyone sharing a parent counts as a brother or sister), with “+ Parent”, “+ Partner”, “+ Brother or sister” and “+ Child”: someone already in the bible, or a new character opened with its name ready to type.

“See the family tree”: the whole family drawn by generation, partners side by side (two lines for a marriage), lines down to their children. Click anyone to open their page. A wide tree shrinks to fit; wider still, Shift and the mouse wheel move across it.
Characters lists the bible's families (“The Wren family · 7”), each opening its tree. Families are named after the surname most of them share.
A character's Race lists only your own races: the bible's Races and the races you've written on characters. There's no built-in list of elves, dwarves and so on any more.
“New race…” in the Race list makes a race in the bible and opens it with its name ready to type.

Entry pages in the world bible: each kind has its sections (a character: Appearance & personality, Backstory & goals, Abilities & powers, Age, birth & status). Written sections show on the page in full; the rest wait under “Still to write” — click one to write it in the panel.
Change the sections every page of a kind has (“Change the sections every Character page has…”): one per line, for the whole world. Writing already in a section you take out stays on the page.
Notes per book: what happens to an entry in each book, written for one book at a time and shown on its page under the book's name.
A gallery in every entry: add pictures of it (art, sketches, references), caption them, and choose which is the main picture.
Image boards inside entries: “+ New board” on an entry's page makes a board kept there, not in the sidebar. A board from the sidebar can be moved onto an entry's page from its panel (“Kept in”).
Merging two copies of an entry keeps both sets of sections, pictures and book notes.

The world bible tidies itself: copies of one entry (the same name, either apostrophe) are merged into one, keeping every name, detail, picture and relationship. The merged copies go to the Trash, so one can be brought back. A character and a creature of the same name become one character that is that creature.
When a book joins a world, its own bible entries move into the world's bible (merging any it already has).
Fixed: “Add to the bible” in Review › Names could add the same name again and again.

“Check these kinds”: entries that look filed under the wrong kind are pointed out (Zornov's race is Demon, so Demon reads like a race), with “Make it a Race” or “Keep it”. Right-click any entry's card to change its kind.

Creatures, one level at a time: each species as a card; click it for its kinds; click a kind for the named characters of that kind. A path back up at the top, “+ Add a kind”, and drag a card onto another to move it under it. A character can be a creature too (“A creature?” on its page).
Bigger gender and sex signs on character cards and group headings.

The cover designer works for every edition. For a paperback, hardback or large print edition it makes the whole print cover (back, spine and front) at that edition's trim size and spine width, with 0.125 in bleed, as a print-ready PDF at 300 pixels per inch.

The back cover carries your blurb (it starts as the book's synopsis) and keeps a white space for the ISBN barcode the printer adds; the spine has the title and author once it's wide enough for words (0.25 in).
Easier to find: “Design a cover…” under the cover in a book's details, “Design the print cover…” in Spine and cover, and a link in Publishing's sidebar for whichever edition is open.
“Use the front as the ebook cover” makes the matching 1600 × 2560 ebook cover from the same design.

Design a cover: Publishing › Cover and look › “Design a cover…” makes an ebook cover from the title, author and series line, at 1600 × 2560 pixels (the size ebook stores ask for). Four layouts (Classic frame, Picture, Picture and band, Minimal), seven colour sets, your own picture if you like, and the typeface. The design is kept, so the cover can be changed later.

EPUBs look like the printed book: chapters open as in your Typesetting design (“Chapter One” over the title, or a large number), with the drop cap and first words in small capitals if you chose them, your own scene-break symbol, and left-aligned text if you set that. Prologues and front matter are never numbered.
The book's typeface goes inside the ebook (with its licence), and the copyright page says what it's set in. Readers can still choose their own.
A choice of spaced paragraphs with no indent, for non-fiction ebooks.
The cover fills the screen on every e-reader, whatever its shape.
“Read it as an ebook” shows the same styling as the EPUB.

Review copies for beta readers: Review › Comments › “Make a review copy…” saves the book as one web page. Your reader opens it in any browser, selects words to comment on them (or comments on a whole chapter), and sends you back the small file it makes. “Import a reader’s comments…” puts each comment on the words it was about, with the reader’s name.
Messages and questions (“Delete this?”, “Saved”) now appear in a NorthRay dialog that matches the app, instead of the plain grey Windows box.
Clearer top bar: the tabs you're not on are brighter against the night sky.
Words and names with apostrophes (Zah’mes, Brennick’s) can be added to the dictionary and match the bible, whichever apostrophe you type (’ or ').
Ctrl+Backspace and Ctrl+Delete remove a whole word at a time.
Page width has a new “Fit” setting: the text fills the window.
Long words move whole to the next line; the editor never breaks a word with a hyphen.
Fixed: Enter in a bulleted or numbered list didn't start a new item.
Text on the night sky stays clear: stars keep away from the words in title bars and sidebars.

Fancy dialogue tags are marked far less: an action as a tag only when a comma joins it to the speech (“Fine,” she smiled), never after a question, an exclamation or a full stop (“What’s the matter, Blue?” I sighed / “We need this.” I laughed).
Groups and races have Members: the people (and creatures) in them as cards, "+ Add members…" to tick them in and out, and a cross to take one out.

Characters can be grouped by gender or sex, by race, or not at all (Group by, at the top of Characters). Creatures are split by their top-level kind (Dragon: the dragon, its types and the dragons themselves).
Fixed: the fix buttons on style hints ("Change to…", "Remove…", rewrites) didn't change anything. They all work now.

Fancy dialogue tags and tag adverbs are only marked on real tags, verbs attached to the speech (“Go,” he hissed / She hissed, “Go.”), not actions after it (“Then I just-” Bluebolt roared; “Fine.” I laughed warmly). And only when it's overdone: an action as a tag (she smiled), the same tag a third time, or six or more and over twice the plain ones.
"seemed to know" is offered as "knew" instead of being cut.

Creatures are a family tree of your own: each can be "A kind of" another creature in the bible (Dragon › Glimmerwyrm › Bluebolt). They nest that way in Worldbuilding, and your top-level kinds are filters in the sidebar. The fixed list of creature types is gone.

The Writing Studio now has the NorthRay look, like the Launcher, Browser and Files: a new icon (an open book under the aurora and the north star), the night sky and aurora along the top with the NorthRay mark, and NorthRay's cool colours with aurora green in the app and the writing page, in light and dark. Everything works as before.

Comic scripts: set a book's Format to "Comic script" (its details panel). Writing then has Page, Panel, Dialogue, Caption and SFX (style menu, or Alt+1 to Alt+5); typing "PAGE ", "PANEL ", "CAPTION: ", "SFX: " or a name and a colon ("TOM: ") starts that kind of line, and Enter moves on to the likely next one. Pages, panels and balloons are numbered for you as you write: PAGE ONE (right · two panels), Panel 1, 1. CAPTION:, 2. TOM:.

The "Comic script" typesetting design sets the script the way artists and letterers expect: Courier Prime on US Letter, each comic page on a new page, panels and balloons numbered, names in bold capitals. Export it from Typesetting as a PDF.
The world bible is grouped by the book each entry first appears in, in series reading order ("Not in a book yet" last). Places inside other places sit with them, marked "in …".
Characters are split by gender or sex within each book, with a sign on each card.
Races and Realms are categories in the bible. A character's race and realm (and a place's or creature's realm) are chosen from the bible's own; choosing a common one it doesn't have yet adds it.
The small text links are now proper buttons.

Every kind of style hint now explains itself and suggests a fix: break a long sentence at a natural point, start a "There was" sentence with its subject, rewrite "was eaten by the dog" as "the dog ate", join repeated sentence starts, swap "said quietly" for "whispered", and filter words come with an example of showing instead.
Fancy dialogue tags are only marked when it's overdone: tags that are actions ("she smiled"), more fancy tags than plain ones, or the same one again and again.
Spelling suggestions catch jumbled letters ("Capitan" → "Captain") and words written as one ("alot" → "a lot").

Worldbuilding: a new Creatures kind; characters can be filtered by gender or sex, race, and realm; places by type and realm; creatures by type. Choose them in the details panel; what you've already written as "Gender:" or "Race:" lines counts.
Each kind of entry has its own colour, on the Worldbuilding cards, in the name links in your text and on the name cards.
Relationships suit the kind of entry: a place offers "Located in", "Borders", "Capital of" and "Home of" rather than family ties, and the entries that fit come first.

Review › Names: "Change to …" corrects a name everywhere in the book (the old text stays in each chapter's versions); "Add to the bible" asks what kind of entry it is. Names with curly apostrophes (Zah’mes) now match the bible, and word forms (Fluxian, Elven) aren't taken for misspellings.
"Show it" and Appears in open the chapter with the name highlighted and scrolled into view.
Front matter and back matter: a chapter-level section can be marked as either (Kind in its details). They're never numbered, so Chapter 1 stays Chapter 1, and front matter keeps roman page numbers.
Typesetting keeps the symbols you use for point of view (✧, 🗡, 🪶, ★): characters the book font doesn't have come from bundled symbol fonts (Noto, OFL) instead of empty boxes.
Hide the outline or the details panel for more room: the two buttons beside Settings, or F3 and F4.
Links look cleaner: no underlines, a soft highlight when you point at them.

Style hints offer fixes you can click: remove a doubled word, a filler word or a dialogue-tag adverb; change a fancy tag to "said" or "asked"; plainer phrasings for clichés ("in the nick of time" → "just in time"); "began to run" → "ran"; the spelling or dash the chapter mostly uses; and your own rules' replacements.
Echoes suggest other words and phrases to use instead, and can show you the earlier use.

A thesaurus: select a word or a phrase (or put the cursor in a word) and press ≈ on the toolbar or Ctrl+Shift+O for other ways to say it, in the same form ("passed away" → "died", "kicked the bucket"). Built from WordNet, works offline.
Spelling suggestions reach words that are several letters off ("skelingtons" suggests "skeletons", "definately" suggests "definitely"), not just one-letter slips.

Long names skip middle names too: "Albus Percival Wulfric Brian Dumbledore" links as Albus Dumbledore, Albus Brian Dumbledore and so on, as long as the first or last name is there. A middle name on its own still doesn't link.

Characters' names link by their first or last name on their own, or by runs that include one of them: for "Snarf Jill Grave", Snarf, Grave, Snarf Grave, Snarf Jill and Jill Grave all link, but Jill alone doesn't (a middle name is rarely used by itself). Names written in capitals ("JACKSON!") are found too.

A spell checker of the Studio's own, with British or American English dictionaries to match the book's language. It knows every name in your bible, accepts Oxford -ize spellings in British English, and keeps a dictionary for each world (or independent book). Hover a mistake for suggestions (click one to use it), Add to the dictionary, or Ignore once. Your added words are listed with your style rules.
Fixed: style hints could stay switched off after updating. They're now on (Full) unless you chose Off.

Worldbuilding pages link to each other like a wiki: names of other entries in a summary, details or notes are links (a name shared by several offers a choice), and each page lists the entries that mention it under Linked from.

Image boards: boards of pictures for a world or an independent book (characters, maps, places, moods). Drag pictures anywhere, resize them by the corner, caption them, tie them to an entry (and use one as the entry's picture). Pictures are kept in the library and listed in Artwork.

Planning has three views. Corkboard: your chapters and scenes as index cards pinned to a cork board (the pin is the status). Drag a card beside another to move it before or after, or onto the middle of a chapter to make a scene part of it.

Timeline: place chapters and scenes on the story's own calendar (days, weeks, months or years, plus words such as "Midsummer, 1204"), in a lane for each viewpoint character. Drag a card along to move it in time. A line joins them in reading order and turns orange where the story jumps back, so flashbacks stand out.

Structure: lay a story shape over the book (three acts, fifteen beats, the hero's journey, seven points, five acts or kishōtenketsu). The book is shown by length with each beat marked, each beat says which chapter falls there, and you can match beats to chapters and see whether yours come early or late. An empty book can be outlined from a structure in one step.

Characters' names link by their parts too: "Maren Ada Holt" is also found as Maren, Holt or Maren Holt (titles and words such as "of" don't count on their own). When characters share a name, it links to all of them and its card shows each one. Worldbuilding's "Appears in" and the cards' cast use the same rule, and a full name is no longer counted twice.
Fixed: choosing from a menu opened by a button could act on the wrong item, or close the Studio.
Every pop-up menu (right-click menus, and choices such as an entry's kind or a chapter's status) now has the NorthRay look, in light or dark, instead of the plain Windows menu.
Hover a name from your Worldbuilding bible in the text to see its card: picture (or initials), name, kind, other names, summary and the first few details, with Open in Worldbuilding.

Style hints, rebuilt: they now tell dialogue from narration, so characters can talk naturally. New kinds: echoes (the same word again within a few lines), repeated sentence starts, adverbs on dialogue tags, fancy dialogue tags, redundancies ("nodded his head"), clichés, and mixed spellings or dash styles. Names from your bible are never counted as echoes.

Hints have three modes: Off, Quiet (only clear slips, the new default) and Full. Click the hint count in the editor's toolbar to turn each kind on or off, see how many are in the chapter, jump from one to the next, and see a reading-ease figure.
Hover a hint to see why it's marked, with Ignore once, Ignore it everywhere in this world, or Turn off this kind.

Your own style rules, kept with the world (or with the book when it isn't in a world): flag words, suggest a replacement, limit how often a word is used, flag a word used again too soon, keep to one spelling of a name, or, for experts, a pattern (run safely, so it can never freeze the editor). Each shows how many times it matches in the open chapter as you make it. Rules can be exported and imported as files to share.
No more status bar along the bottom of the window. Messages appear for a moment as a small note near the bottom instead. Today's words are at the foot of the outline while you write.
A Writing view panel (Aa in the editor's toolbar): Serif, Book, Sans or Typewriter type, four sizes, and a narrow, normal or wide page. Your choices are remembered.
Focus mode (Ctrl+Shift+F): the outline and details panel step aside, and everything but the paragraph you're in fades back.
Typewriter scrolling (Ctrl+Shift+T): the line you're typing stays near the middle of the window.
Spell check can be turned off and on (it uses Windows' own dictionaries; right-click a word for suggestions).
Style hints (off until you turn them on): doubled words, filler words, maybe-passive verbs and long sentences get a gentle underline. Hover one to see why. They never change your text.
Names from your Worldbuilding bible are linked in the text: Ctrl+click one to open its page.

Backups: a copy every 30 minutes while you work (when something changed) and when you close the Studio, as well as when the library opens. In Settings you can have them copied to a second folder too, such as another drive or a synced folder.

Minimise, maximise and close are now part of the app's own top area, like NorthRay Browser, instead of a separate Windows title bar. Drag the empty part of the top to move the window; double-click it to maximise. On Windows 11, pointing at maximise shows the snap layouts.
Maintenance release.
Maintenance release.

Comments: select some words and choose Comment (✎) in the toolbar, or press Ctrl+Alt+M, to leave a note on them. A chapter's details list its comments, and Review has a Comments section for the whole book.
Resolve a comment once it's dealt with: it stays with its words, unhighlighted, and can be reopened. Comments never appear in the PDF or EPUB.
The "preview" notes are gone from the About box, Settings, Typesetting and Publishing, which now say what the Studio includes.
Maintenance release, with screenshots of the Studio in NorthRay Launcher and on the website.
Settings are read more carefully: a setting saved by another version can no longer stop the Studio starting.
Maintenance release.

Review (new): compare any chapter or scene with an earlier version or a snapshot. Added words are shaded and removed words struck through, with counts, and you can restore the older text (the current one is kept, so it can be undone).
Snapshots: save the whole book as it is (before a revision, before sending it to an editor) and see later which chapters changed and by how much. Snapshots are kept until you remove them.

Names: a continuity check finds spellings close to a name in the world's bible (“Marren” for “Maren”) and names used often that aren't in it yet. Add one as another name, add it to the bible, or mark it as fine.
Goals: set a daily word goal and see today's words, the last 7 and 28 days, your streak, and a chart of each day. Writing's status bar shows today's progress.
Libraries are upgraded automatically.

Planning (new): the Planning tab shows every chapter and scene as a card on a board, in the order of the book and grouped by part. Each card shows its status (with a coloured edge), synopsis, viewpoint character, and words against its target.
Cards show which characters appear in each chapter and scene, found in the text from the world's bible.
Word targets for the book and for each chapter or scene, with progress in the sidebar and on the cards. Filter the board by status: outline, draft, revised or final.
Choose a chapter's or scene's viewpoint character from the world's characters. The panel lists every entry that appears in it, linked to Worldbuilding.
Move cards earlier or later, add chapters and scenes, and open any of them in Writing. Libraries are upgraded automatically.
Worldbuilding (new): every world keeps a bible of characters, places, groups, things, lore and events, shared by all its books. Independent books get their own.
Each entry has other names it goes by, a summary, a picture, a list of details (Age: 34, Eyes: grey), and notes.
Relationships between entries read correctly from both sides: “Lives in Highcliff” on a character shows as “Home of” on the place.
Appears in: each entry lists the chapters and scenes its name (or another name it goes by) appears in, with how often and the first time in context. Click one to open it in Writing.
A world's page in the Library summarises its entries. Entries go to the Trash and can be restored.

Editions (new): each book can have a paperback, hardback, large-print and ebook edition, each with its own ISBN. Print editions can have their own trim size and design; a new large-print edition starts with the large-print design.
Publishing works one edition at a time: print editions get their checks, spine and cover measurements, a print-ready PDF and a proof; the ebook edition gets the EPUB.
The copyright page, in print and in the EPUB, lists every edition's ISBN.
Checks fit the edition: no print checks for the ebook, no ebook cover check for print, and a warning if two editions share an ISBN.
Existing books get a paperback (with the book's ISBN and its publishing settings) and an ebook edition the first time Publishing opens them. Libraries are upgraded automatically.
Publishing (new): the Publishing tab checks the book, gives the measurements for its cover, and makes the files for printers and ebook stores.

Print-ready PDF in the PDF/X-1a format print-on-demand printers ask for: text in pure black, pictures in grey (or CMYK for a colour interior), fonts embedded, and an optional 0.125-inch bleed on the outside edges.

EPUB 3 ebook export, with an EPUB 2 contents file for older readers: cover, title and copyright pages, a contents list with parts and chapters, pictures cropped and sized for e-readers, and accessibility information. It uses the same chapters as the Preview.
Pre-flight checks: missing author, description or cover; an ISBN with a wrong check digit; pictures without a description, or that would print blurred; too few pages for a paperback.
Spine width for white or cream paper, and the full cover size with bleed, for your cover designer. Check them against your printer's own cover template before the cover is finished.

Preview (new): see the book as an ebook on a phone, a 6-inch e-ink reader or a tablet. Turn pages by clicking or with the arrow keys, and try the reader's own settings: white, sepia or night pages, text size, and the book's typeface, a serif or a sans-serif.
Typesetting: zoom (fit, actual size, 200%), single pages as well as spreads, and guides showing the margins, the baseline grid and the spine edge.
Typesetting: chapter openings with “Chapter One” above the title, or a large numeral; drop caps; front matter numbered i, ii, iii, with the story starting at page 1 on a right-hand page.
Chapters already titled “Chapter 3: …” keep their number; prologues, acknowledgements and the like aren't numbered.
Typesetting: a contents page with page numbers (parts in small capitals, chapters indented).
Typesetting: a copyright page on the back of the title page, made only from the book's own details (author, edition, ISBN); with none of those it stays blank.
Typesetting: chapters can open with their first words in small capitals.
Typesetting: margin controls (inside, outside, top and bottom).
Exported PDFs are much smaller: only the letters used are embedded.
PDF import: a title page in large type stays front matter instead of becoming chapters; “CHAPTER ONE” joins the title on the line below it; placeholder details such as “unspecified” are ignored.
Typesetting (new): the Typesetting tab sets your whole book as printed pages and shows them as two-page spreads. Text is justified and hyphenated, with real kerning, ligatures and small capitals.
Paragraphs are set as a whole (the Knuth–Plass method TeX uses), so spacing stays even. Widows and orphans are prevented, and chapters open part-way down a new page.
Pages include a title page, part pages, running heads (book title on the left, chapter on the right), page numbers, scene breaks, and your pictures with their crops and captions.

Four starting designs (Classic, Open, Ragged right, Large print), plus typeface, type size, line spacing, trim size, justified or ragged text, hyphenation, chapters on right-hand pages, running heads and title page. Each book remembers its design.
Export the typeset book as a PDF with the fonts embedded and text that can be searched and copied. Print-ready PDF/X for printers comes with publishing.
Bundled book fonts: Crimson Text and Gentium Book (SIL Open Font License). British and US English hyphenation.

Artwork library: a new Artwork page lists every picture in your library, stored once however many chapters use it. Add pictures, name them, mark them as a map, illustration, ornament and so on, and see which chapters use each one.
Pictures in the text can be cropped, sized and aligned from the details panel: drag the frame or its corners to crop. The stored picture is never changed, so a crop can always be undone.
Print checks: each picture shows its printed size and resolution for the book's trim size, with a warning below 300 ppi and a stronger one below 150, and a one-click size that prints sharply.
Books have a trim size (6 × 9 in, A5, B-format and more), and measurements can be shown in inches, centimetres, millimetres or pixels (Settings).
New pictures start at the widest size that prints sharply. Pictures that came with imported books are listed in the artwork library too.
+ Scene now adds a *** divider at the end of the chapter, with the cursor ready for the new scene, instead of a separate page.
Captions and screen-reader descriptions for pictures.

No more Windows menu bar: every command has a place in the window. A new Settings page (in the top bar, or Ctrl+,) holds the library folder, export and backup, the theme and a full list of keyboard shortcuts; New book and Import sit on the Library page; Move to Trash is in the details panel; the editor toolbar has previous and next chapter buttons.
Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down move to the previous or next chapter, from the text or the outline.
Saving... then Saved, in the editor and the status bar, so you can see your words are stored.
The Studio reopens the book and chapter you were working on.
Double-click a book to open it in Writing. New chapters, scenes and parts start with their title selected; press Enter to go straight to the text.
An empty chapter shows a faint prompt; a new library offers Create a book and Import a book.
One details panel layout for books, chapters and scenes, in tidy sections; the outline lines up with the Library sidebar.
The import preview fits the window, and switching chapters no longer flickers.
No scroll bars anywhere, including the longer text boxes; the wheel and keys still scroll.

Word (.docx) and OpenDocument (.odt) import: chapters from heading styles (or from lines like "CHAPTER ONE" when there are none), parts, italic, bold, small caps, quotes, lists, pictures, links, footnotes (gathered into Notes) and the document's title and author. Tracked changes come in as accepted.
Fixed: some documents' formatting was ignored when it was set through their styles.
Smoother animations: eased page changes, status messages that fade in and out, and softer hover effects.
Book covers lift slightly on hover; the workspace tabs, sidebar and outline highlights slide to your choice; the import tick boxes animate.
The Bookshelf/List switch no longer overlaps the filter button.
Fixes the Studio closing while importing: files are now read by a separate helper process, so a file the importer can't handle shows an explanation instead of closing the app.
Unexpected errors while reading or importing are explained rather than closing the app.
If the Studio ever does close unexpectedly, it notes where in crash.log (in %LOCALAPPDATA%\NorthRay\Writing Studio) so the cause can be found.
The Writing workspace: parts, chapters and scenes in an outline you can drag to rearrange, with word counts and a status for each.

A page-like editor with paragraph styles (Body, First paragraph, Centred, Epigraph, Attribution, Verse, Letter, Note, headings), bold, italic, underline, small caps, scene breaks, quotes, lists and pictures.
Saves as you type; keeps an earlier version of each chapter and scene every ten minutes or so (the last 40), which you can restore.

Import from EPUB (parts, chapters, front and back matter, styling, pictures, title, author and cover), HTML, Markdown and plain text, with a preview to choose what comes in. DRM-protected books are refused.
PDF import (experimental): chapters and paragraphs are worked out from the page layout, so check the result.
Subtle animations throughout, and hidden scroll bars.
First preview (Milestone 1): the Author Library.
Worlds, series and books, including standalone books and books outside any world.
Separate reading and chronological order for every series; drag and drop to reorder or move.
Covers, world banners and logos; details edited in a side panel that saves as you type.
A safe local library: every change saved at once, a backup each time it opens, the Trash, and JSON export.
